claim: From 1985 to 2016, the prevalence of underweight decreased in most regions.
source: From 1985 to 2016, the prevalence of underweight decreased, and that of obesity and severe obesity increased, in most regions, with significant variation in the magnitude of these changes across regions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of findings from the analysis of 2896 population-based studies with 187 million participants.

claim: From 1985 to 2016, the prevalence of obesity increased in most regions.
source: From 1985 to 2016, the prevalence of underweight decreased, and that of obesity and severe obesity increased, in most regions, with significant variation in the magnitude of these changes across regions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of findings from the analysis of 2896 population-based studies with 187 million participants.

claim: From 1985 to 2016, the prevalence of severe obesity increased in most regions.
source: From 1985 to 2016, the prevalence of underweight decreased, and that of obesity and severe obesity increased, in most regions, with significant variation in the magnitude of these changes across regions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of findings from the analysis of 2896 population-based studies with 187 million participants.

claim: There is significant variation in the magnitude of changes in underweight, obesity, and severe obesity prevalence across regions from 1985 to 2016.
source: From 1985 to 2016, the prevalence of underweight decreased, and that of obesity and severe obesity increased, in most regions, with significant variation in the magnitude of these changes across regions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of findings from the analysis of 2896 population-based studies with 187 million participants.

claim: Changes in the prevalence of underweight and total obesity are largely driven by shifts in the distribution of BMI.
source: Changes in the prevalence of underweight and total obesity, and to a lesser extent severe obesity, are largely driven by shifts in the distribution of BMI, with smaller contributions from changes in the shape of the distribution.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract based on the analysis of the relationship between mean BMI and prevalence.

claim: Changes in the prevalence of severe obesity are driven by shifts in the distribution of BMI to a lesser extent than underweight and total obesity.
source: Changes in the prevalence of underweight and total obesity, and to a lesser extent severe obesity, are largely driven by shifts in the distribution of BMI, with smaller contributions from changes in the shape of the distribution.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract based on the analysis of the relationship between mean BMI and prevalence.

claim: Changes in the shape of the BMI distribution make smaller contributions to changes in underweight and obesity prevalence compared to shifts in the distribution.
source: Changes in the prevalence of underweight and total obesity, and to a lesser extent severe obesity, are largely driven by shifts in the distribution of BMI, with smaller contributions from changes in the shape of the distribution.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract based on the analysis of the relationship between mean BMI and prevalence.

claim: In East and Southeast Asia, the underweight tail of the BMI distribution was left behind as the distribution shifted.
source: In East and Southeast Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, the underweight tail of the BMI distribution was left behind as the distribution shifted.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the analysis of regional BMI distribution changes.

claim: In sub-Saharan Africa, the underweight tail of the BMI distribution was left behind as the distribution shifted.
source: In East and Southeast Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, the underweight tail of the BMI distribution was left behind as the distribution shifted.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the analysis of regional BMI distribution changes.

claim: There is a need for policies that address all forms of malnutrition by making healthy foods accessible and affordable.
source: There is a need for policies that address all forms of malnutrition by making healthy foods accessible and affordable, while restricting unhealthy foods through fiscal and regulatory restrictions.
evidence: This is a policy recommendation stated in the abstract based on the study findings.

claim: There is a need for policies that restrict unhealthy foods through fiscal and regulatory restrictions.
source: There is a need for policies that address all forms of malnutrition by making healthy foods accessible and affordable, while restricting unhealthy foods through fiscal and regulatory restrictions.
evidence: This is a policy recommendation stated in the abstract based on the study findings.

claim: Underweight can lead to adverse health outcomes.
source: Underweight as well as obesity can lead to adverse health outcomes (Prospective Studies Collaboration et al., 2009; Global BMI Mortality Collaboration, 2016; Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Obesity can lead to adverse health outcomes.
source: Underweight as well as obesity can lead to adverse health outcomes (Prospective Studies Collaboration et al., 2009; Global BMI Mortality Collaboration, 2016; Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: For at least four decades, the prevalence of underweight has decreased in most countries.
source: For at least four decades, the prevalence of underweight has decreased, and that of obesity has increased, in most countries with significant variation in the magnitude of these changes across regions of the world (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2017a; NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous NCD-RisC studies.

claim: For at least four decades, the prevalence of obesity has increased in most countries.
source: For at least four decades, the prevalence of underweight has decreased, and that of obesity has increased, in most countries with significant variation in the magnitude of these changes across regions of the world (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2017a; NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous NCD-RisC studies.

claim: A shift in the whole distribution of BMI would simultaneously affect mean BMI as well as the prevalence of underweight and obesity.
source: A shift in the whole distribution of body mass index (BMI) would simultaneously affect mean BMI as well as the prevalence of underweight and obesity (Razak et al., 2018; Rose and Day, 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Changes in the shape of BMI distribution would affect the prevalence of underweight and obesity with only small impacts on the population mean.
source: In contrast, changes in the shape of BMI distribution – for example, widening or narrowing of the BMI distribution, becoming more or less skewed, or having a thinner or thicker tail – would affect the prevalence of underweight and obesity with only small impacts on the population mean, as shown schematically in Figure 1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Understanding the mechanisms of BMI distribution change is essential as they may require different public health and clinical responses.
source: Understanding these two mechanisms is essential as they may require different public health and clinical responses (Penman and Johnson, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: It is unclear how much the two mechanisms (shift vs. shape change) have contributed to the observed decline in underweight and rise in obesity in different world regions.
source: But it is unclear how much the two mechanisms have contributed to the observed decline in underweight and rise in obesity in different world regions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: The NCD-RisC database contains 2896 population-based studies conducted from 1985 to 2019 with height and weight measurements of 187 million participants.
source: The Non-Communicable Disease Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC) database contains 2896 population-based studies conducted from 1985 to 2019 with height and weight measurements of 187 million participants.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the data sources.

claim: 2033 studies in the NCD-RisC database had measurements of height and weight on 132.6 million participants aged 20–79 years.
source: Of these, 2033 studies had measurements of height and weight on 132.6 million participants aged 20–79 years.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the data sources.

source: The number of studies with participants aged 20–79 years in different regions ranged from 53 in Oceania to 637 in the high-income western region.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the data sources.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing regional prevalence patterns in 2016.

claim: In 2016, the age-standardised prevalence of obesity was highest (>24%) in Central and Eastern Europe; the high-income western region; Latin America and the Caribbean; Oceania; and Central Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa for most age and sex groups.

claim: In 2016, the age-standardised prevalence of severe obesity was lowest (<2%) in South Asia; East and Southeast Asia; the high-income Asia Pacific region; and men in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: It was lowest (<2%) in South Asia; East and Southeast Asia; the high-income Asia Pacific region; and men in sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing regional prevalence patterns in 2016.

claim: The prevalence of obesity increased from 1985 to 2016 in all regions.

claim: The prevalence of severe obesity increased from 1985 to 2016 in all regions.
source: The prevalence of underweight decreased or stayed unchanged and that of obesity and severe obesity increased from 1985 to 2016 in all regions, with the exception of an increase in the prevalence of underweight in younger women in the high-income Asia Pacific region.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing trends from 1985 to 2016.

source: The largest absolute decrease in underweight prevalence from 1985 to 2016 was seen in South Asia; East and Southeast Asia; and sub-Saharan Africa, where it declined by 14–35 percentage points in different age–sex groups (Figure 4).

claim: Underweight prevalence remained higher in South Asia, East and Southeast Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa than elsewhere in 2016.

source: Prevalence of underweight changed only marginally in regions such as Central and Eastern Europe and the high-income western region, where prevalence was already low in 1985.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing trends from 1985 to 2016.

source: The largest absolute increase in obesity prevalence from 1985 to 2016 occurred in Central Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa; the high-income western region; Latin America and the Caribbean; Oceania (women); and Central and Eastern Europe (men) (Figure 4).

source: In these regions and sexes, obesity prevalence increased by 16–24 percentage points in different age groups, and severe obesity increased by 5–13 percentage points.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing trends from 1985 to 2016.

source: The increase in obesity was less than five percentage points in the high-income Asia Pacific region; South Asia; and in men in sub-Saharan Africa

source: These indicate that 93% (men) and 96% (women) of variation in obesity, and between 83% and 92% of variation in underweight and severe obesity, were explained by mean BMI and other variables (year, region, and age group) in the regression models.

claim: Between 83% and 92% of variation in underweight and severe obesity were explained by mean BMI and other variables (year, region, and age group) in the regression models.
source: These indicate that 93% (men) and 96% (women) of variation in obesity, and between 83% and 92% of variation in underweight and severe obesity, were explained by mean BMI and other variables (year, region, and age group) in the regression models.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the regression analysis results.

claim: For all three outcomes (underweight, obesity, severe obesity), the association of prevalence with mean BMI varied across regions.
source: For all three outcomes, the association of prevalence with mean BMI varied across regions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the regression analysis results.

claim: The inter-regional variation in the prevalence–mean association was stronger for obesity and severe obesity than underweight.
source: The inter-regional variation in the prevalence–mean association was stronger for obesity and severe obesity than underweight, as seen in larger inter-regional range of the interaction terms.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the regression analysis results.

claim: The rise in mean BMI accounted for >82% of the decline in underweight in different age–sex groups in South Asia.
source: The rise in mean BMI accounted for >82% of the decline in underweight in different age–sex groups in South Asia, where underweight prevalence declined by over 16 percentage points for all age–sex groups (Figure 5).

claim: In South Asia, underweight prevalence declined by over 16 percentage points for all age–sex groups from 1985 to 2016.
source: The rise in mean BMI accounted for >82% of the decline in underweight in different age–sex groups in South Asia, where underweight prevalence declined by over 16 percentage points for all age–sex groups (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: In South Asia, the remainder of the decline in underweight beyond the effects of mean BMI was due to change in the shape of the BMI distribution which reduced underweight prevalence.
source: The remainder of the decline was due to change in the shape of the BMI distribution which reduced underweight prevalence beyond the effects of the population mean.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the contribution of mean BMI to changes in underweight.

claim: In sub-Saharan Africa and East and Southeast Asia, the total change in prevalence of underweight (3–12 percentage points) was 20–80% less than what was expected based on the increase in mean BMI.
source: In contrast, in sub-Saharan Africa and East and Southeast Asia, the total change in prevalence of underweight (3–12 percentage points) was 20–80% less than what was expected based on the increase in mean BMI (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Where obesity increased the most (Central Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa; Latin America and the Caribbean; and the high-income western region), the rise in mean BMI accounted for over three quarters of the increase in different age–sex groups.
source: Where obesity increased the most – Central Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa; Latin America and the Caribbean; and the high-income western region – the rise in mean BMI accounted for over three quarters of the increase in different age–sex groups (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: In Oceania, the actual rise in prevalence of obesity (8–14 percentage points for all age–sex groups) was about two-thirds to one-half of what would have been expected by the observed increase in mean BMI in men and women.
source: In Oceania, the actual rise in prevalence of obesity (8–14 percentage points for all age–sex groups) was about two-thirds to one-half of what would have been expected by the observed increase in mean BMI in men and women (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Change in mean BMI consistently accounted for a smaller share of the change in severe obesity than it did for change in total obesity.
source: Change in mean BMI consistently accounted for a smaller share of the change in severe obesity than it did for change in total obesity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the contribution of mean BMI to changes in obesity.

claim: In regions where prevalence of severe obesity changed by more than one percentage point, the contribution of change in mean BMI to change in severe obesity in different regions was 53–90% of the corresponding contribution for total obesity.
source: Specifically, in regions where prevalence of severe obesity changed by more than one percentage point, the contribution of change in mean BMI to change in severe obesity in different regions was 53–90% of the corresponding contribution for total obesity (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The trends in the prevalence of underweight, total obesity, and, to a lesser extent, severe obesity are largely driven by shifts in the distribution of BMI, with smaller contributions from changes in the shape of the distribution.
source: We found that the trends in the prevalence of underweight, total obesity, and, to a lesser extent, severe obesity are largely driven by shifts in the distribution of BMI, with smaller contributions from changes in the shape of the distribution.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the main findings.

claim: The decline in the prevalence of underweight in East and Southeast Asia was smaller than expected based on change in mean BMI.
source: The notable exceptions to this pattern were the decline in the prevalence of underweight in East and Southeast Asia and sub-Saharan Africa and the rise of obesity in Oceania, which were both smaller than expected based on change in mean BMI.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the main findings.

claim: The decline in the prevalence of underweight in sub-Saharan Africa was smaller than expected based on change in mean BMI.

evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the main findings.

claim: The rise of obesity in Oceania was smaller than expected based on change in mean BMI.
source: The notable exceptions to this pattern were the decline in the prevalence of underweight in East and Southeast Asia and sub-Saharan Africa and the rise of obesity in Oceania, which were both smaller than expected based on change in mean BMI.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the main findings.

claim: The study results are consistent with a recent cross-sectional study using data from women in low- and middle-income countries that found a strong association between mean BMI and prevalence of obesity, and a moderate association between mean BMI and prevalence of underweight.
source: Our results are consistent with a recent cross-sectional study (Razak et al., 2018) using data from women in low- and middle-income countries that found a strong association between mean BMI and prevalence of obesity, and a moderate association between mean BMI and prevalence of underweight.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing the study results to previous research.

claim: The study results are consistent with another study which found that changes in median BMI contributed more than 75% to the increase in obesity in the USA from 1980 to 2000.
source: Our results are also consistent with another study which found that changes in median BMI contributed more than 75% to the increase in obesity in the USA from 1980 to 2000 (Helmchen and Henderson, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing the study results to previous research.

claim: The study presents the first global analysis of how much the rise in mean BMI versus changes in the shape of its distribution influenced changes in both underweight and obesity prevalence.
source: the strengths of our study include presenting the first global analysis of how much the rise in mean BMI versus changes in the shape of its distribution influenced changes in both underweight and obesity prevalence.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the study's strengths.

claim: The study used an unprecedented amount of data from different regions covering three decades.
source: We used an unprecedented amount of data from different regions covering three decades and used only measured data on height and weight to avoid biases in self-reported data.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the study's strengths.

claim: The study used only measured data on height and weight to avoid biases in self-reported data.
source: We used an unprecedented amount of data from different regions covering three decades and used only measured data on height and weight to avoid biases in self-reported data.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the study's strengths.

claim: Some regions, especially Oceania and sub-Saharan Africa, had less data, especially early in the analysis period.
source: Despite using the most comprehensive global collection of population-based studies to date, some regions, especially Oceania and sub-Saharan Africa, had less data, especially early in our analysis period.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the study's limitations.

claim: The finding that the majority of the rise in the prevalence of obesity from 1985 to 2016 is mostly the result of a distributional shift points towards an important role for societal drivers.
source: The finding that the majority of the rise in the prevalence of obesity from 1985 to 2016 is mostly the result of a distributional shift points towards an important role for societal drivers, including lower availability and higher price of healthy and fresh foods compared to caloric-dense and nutrient-deficient foods (Swinburn et al., 2011), and mechanisation of work and motorisation of transport throughout the world that have reduced energy expenditure in populations around the world (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2019; Ng and Popkin, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings and supported by citations.

claim: Lower availability and higher price of healthy and fresh foods compared to caloric-dense and nutrient-deficient foods are societal drivers of obesity.
source: The finding that the majority of the rise in the prevalence of obesity from 1985 to 2016 is mostly the result of a distributional shift points towards an important role for societal drivers, including lower availability and higher price of healthy and fresh foods compared to caloric-dense and nutrient-deficient foods (Swinburn et al., 2011), and mechanisation of work and motorisation of transport throughout the world that have reduced energy expenditure in populations around the world (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2019; Ng and Popkin, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings and supported by citations.

claim: Mechanisation of work and motorisation of transport throughout the world have reduced energy expenditure in populations around the world.
source: The finding that the majority of the rise in the prevalence of obesity from 1985 to 2016 is mostly the result of a distributional shift points towards an important role for societal drivers, including lower availability and higher price of healthy and fresh foods compared to caloric-dense and nutrient-deficient foods (Swinburn et al., 2011), and mechanisation of work and motorisation of transport throughout the world that have reduced energy expenditure in populations around the world (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2019; Ng and Popkin, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings and supported by citations.

claim: Although there is a genetic component to BMI at the individual level, genetics explain only a small part of changes over time, especially when people have access to healthy food and living environment.
source: First, although there is a genetic component to BMI at the individual level (Silventoinen et al., 2017; Silventoinen et al., 2016; Locke et al., 2015; Brandkvist et al., 2019), genetics explain only a small part of changes over time, especially when people have access to healthy food and living environment.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings and supported by citations.

claim: When the environment becomes more obesogenic, some people or population subgroups may gain more weight than others, implying that the environment remains the main contributor.
source: When the environment becomes more obesogenic, some people or population subgroups may gain more weight than others, implying that the environment remains the main contributor (Brandkvist et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings and supported by a citation.

claim: The interplay of genetic predisposition and changes in the environment might account for some of the excess rise in obesity and severe obesity beyond the effect of distributional shift alone.
source: This interplay of genetic predisposition and changes in the environment might account for some of the excess rise in obesity and severe obesity beyond the effect of distributional shift alone (Brandkvist et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings and supported by a citation.

claim: In 1985, obesity prevalence in Oceania was already very high.
source: The exception observed in Oceania is possibly because in 1985 obesity prevalence in this region was already so high (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2017a) that the rise in BMI did not change overall obesity status (but there was a substantial increase in those with severe obesity, mostly accounted for by the change in mean BMI).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings and supported by a citation.

claim: In Oceania, the rise in BMI did not change overall obesity status, but there was a substantial increase in those with severe obesity, mostly accounted for by the change in mean BMI.
source: The exception observed in Oceania is possibly because in 1985 obesity prevalence in this region was already so high (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2017a) that the rise in BMI did not change overall obesity status (but there was a substantial increase in those with severe obesity, mostly accounted for by the change in mean BMI).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings.

claim: Underweight is associated with lower socioeconomic status.
source: The smaller decline in underweight than expected in sub-Saharan Africa and East and Southeast Asia may be because underweight is associated with lower socioeconomic status, food insecurity, and for sub-Saharan Africa widening difference between rural and urban BMI levels which is different from other regions (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2019; Brandkvist et al., 2019; Di Cesare et al., 2015; Subramanian and Smith, 2006; Di Cesare et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings and supported by citations.

claim: Underweight is associated with food insecurity.
source: The smaller decline in underweight than expected in sub-Saharan Africa and East and Southeast Asia may be because underweight is associated with lower socioeconomic status, food insecurity, and for sub-Saharan Africa widening difference between rural and urban BMI levels which is different from other regions (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2019; Brandkvist et al., 2019; Di Cesare et al., 2015; Subramanian and Smith, 2006; Di Cesare et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings and supported by citations.

claim: For sub-Saharan Africa, there is a widening difference between rural and urban BMI levels which is different from other regions.
source: The smaller decline in underweight than expected in sub-Saharan Africa and East and Southeast Asia may be because underweight is associated with lower socioeconomic status, food insecurity, and for sub-Saharan Africa widening difference between rural and urban BMI levels which is different from other regions (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2019; Brandkvist et al., 2019; Di Cesare et al., 2015; Subramanian and Smith, 2006; Di Cesare et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings and supported by citations.

claim: If the benefits of economic development do not sufficiently reach the poor, they remain nutritionally vulnerable.
source: If the benefits of economic development do not sufficiently reach the poor, they remain nutritionally vulnerable, as has been seen for height and weight during childhood and adolescence (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2020; Subramanyam et al., 2011; Sanchez and Swaminathan, 2005; Pongou et al., 2006; Haddad, 2003; Stevens et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings and supported by citations.

claim: The rise in mean BMI and obesity together with persistent underweight creates a double burden of malnutrition.
source: Together with the rise in mean BMI and obesity (and short stature which is not a topic of this paper but addressed in other studies) (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2020; Stevens et al., 2012; NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC), 2016a), this creates a double burden of malnutrition (Popkin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting the findings and supported by citations.

claim: The worldwide rise in obesity and the decline in underweight are primarily driven by the shift in the population distribution of BMI.
source: In summary, we found that the worldwide rise in obesity and the decline in underweight are primarily driven by the shift in the population distribution of BMI.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the main findings.

claim: There is evidence of both excess obesity, and especially severe obesity, and persistent underweight beyond the distributional shift in some regions.
source: At the same time, there is an evidence of both excess obesity, and especially severe obesity, and persistent underweight beyond the distributional shift in some regions, which may be related to growing social inequalities that restrict access to healthy foods in those at highest risk of undernutrition (Popkin et al., 2020; Wells et al., 2020; Darmon and Drewnowski, 2015).

claim: Excess obesity and persistent underweight beyond the distributional shift may be related to growing social inequalities that restrict access to healthy foods in those at highest risk of undernutrition.
